title: Example: estimating the distribution of a scan statistic by simulation
text:
The problem
Let \(X_1, X_2, \dots, X_N\) be independent Bernoulli random variables with parameter \(p\). For a window of length \(m\), the one-dimensional discrete scan statistic is
\[
S_m(N) = \max_{1 \le i \le N-m+1} \; \sum_{k=i}^{i+m-1} X_k .
\]
We are interested in \(\mathbb{P}\big(S_m(N) \ge k\big)\), the probability that somewhere in the sequence a window of length \(m\) contains at least \(k\) successes.

Definition 1 (Scan statistic) For a sequence \((X_k)\) and a length \(m\), the scan statistic is the largest number of successes contained in a window of \(m\) consecutive observations.

title: Example: estimating the distribution of a scan statistic by simulation
text:
Monte Carlo estimation in R
The simplest estimator is the relative frequency over a large number of independent simulations:
\[
\widehat{P}_n = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{r=1}^{n} \mathbf{1}\{S^{(r)}_m(N) \ge k\},
\qquad
\operatorname{se}\big(\widehat{P}_n\big) \approx \sqrt{\frac{\widehat{P}_n (1-\widehat{P}_n)}{n}} .
\]
scan_1d <- function(x, m) {
  # window sums of length m, computed from cumulative sums
  s <- cumsum(c(0, x))
  max(s[(m + 1):length(s)] - s[1:(length(s) - m)])
}

set.seed(2026)
N <- 1000; m <- 20; p <- 0.05; k <- 6
S <- replicate(10000, scan_1d(rbinom(N, 1, p), m))

p_hat <- mean(S >= k)
se    <- sqrt(p_hat * (1 - p_hat) / length(S))
c(estimate = p_hat, std_error = se)

text:
Personal webpage

Assistant Professor (Lecturer) and Vice-Dean at the Faculty of Mathematics and Computer Science, University of Bucharest. Senior researcher at the National Institute of Research and Development for Biological Sciences.


I work in mathematical modelling and computational statistics, mainly on scan statistics: sharp approximations and error bounds for detecting clusters and changes in distribution in dependent random fields, with applications in biology, ecology and health.

text:
Activity


Research
Scan statistics for detecting clusters and local changes in one, two and three dimensions, with windows of arbitrary shape and dependent data. Also nonlinear models with bias correction, and models of DNA self-assembly.


Teaching
Probability, statistics and regression at bachelor’s level, statistical tools for finance and biostatistics at master’s level, with R labs. More than 10 master’s dissertations and 20 bachelor’s theses supervised.


Projects
National and European projects in bioinformatics, DNA nanotechnology and environmental science. Director of the institutional development project 2PFE/2021 at NIRDBS.

title: Alexandru Amărioarei
text:
About





I have more than ten years of experience in research and teaching, developing methods of mathematical modelling and computational statistics for complex problems in several applied fields.
I received my PhD in applied mathematics in 2014 from the Laboratoire Paul Painlevé, Université Lille 1, supervised by Prof. Cristian Preda. My thesis gave sharp approximations and error bounds for the distribution of multidimensional discrete scan statistics. During the PhD I was a full member of the MODAL team at Inria Lille – Nord Europe and taught at Polytech’Lille. From September 2016 to February 2017 I returned to Inria as a postdoctoral researcher in the ClinMine project, modelling patients’ pathways through hospitals with functional data analysis.
At the University of Bucharest I teach and supervise theses, and since 2020 I have been Vice-Dean for accreditation, internationalisation and annual reporting. At the National Institute of Research and Development for Biological Sciences I model DNA self-assembly and work with researchers abroad, such as B. Strîmbu on nonlinear models in forestry.

title: Research
text:
TopicsPublicationsTalks




Research topics
My research focuses on scan statistics and the applied probability problems around them. A scan statistic records the largest number of events seen in a window of fixed shape that “scans” a sequence, an image or a volume. It is used to decide whether a cluster of events can be explained by chance.
For a random field \(\{X_{s,t}\}\) on the grid \(\{1,\dots,N_1\}\times\{1,\dots,N_2\}\) and a window of size \(m_1\times m_2\), the two-dimensional discrete scan statistic is
\[
S_{m_1,m_2}(N_1,N_2) \;=\; \max_{\substack{1\le i\le N_1-m_1+1\\ 1\le j\le N_2-m_2+1}} \;\sum_{s=i}^{i+m_1-1}\,\sum_{t=j}^{j+m_2-1} X_{s,t}.
\]
The exact distribution of \(S\) is rarely available, so the focus shifts to accurate approximations with explicit error bounds.
Main directions:

Multidimensional discrete scan statistics. Approximations for the distribution of the scan statistic in two and three dimensions, based on the method of 1-dependent stationary sequences, with error bounds.
Dependent models. Block-factor random fields and models with local dependence, beyond the independence assumption.
Windows of arbitrary shape. Scan statistics whose window can take any shape, which increase the power to detect local changes in models that allow dependent data.
Continuous scan statistics. Approximations for the scan statistic of multidimensional Poisson processes.
Runs and patterns. The distribution of the longest monotone run; the Markov chain imbedding technique.
Simulation methods. Efficient Monte Carlo methods for estimating the distribution of scan statistics.



Applications and collaborations
Beyond scan statistics, my work in mathematical and computational statistical modelling has followed three applied lines:

Uncertainty of nonlinear transformations. With B. Strîmbu (University of Oregon), modelling the uncertainty of nonlinear transformations, which describe relationships within and between systems, and correcting the bias that appears when a transformed variable is back-transformed, for example in forestry practice when the original data are no longer available. The result is an unbiased procedure for modelling complex relationships that is more parsimonious than current approaches.
DNA self-assembly. In the MoDASyS project at the National Institute of Research and Development for Biological Sciences, computational statistical models for a mesh-assembly dynamical system that mimics DNA self-assembly, and a rule-based modelling methodology that gives new insight into the assembly process and its control.
Patient pathways in hospitals. In the ClinMine project at Inria Lille, modelling the dynamics of patients’ pathways through hospitals with functional data analysis.

Other applications include detecting disease clusters (for example, Crohn’s disease) with spatial scan statistics, aquatic ecology and bibliometric assessments of research. See Publications and Projects for details.


Ongoing directions
Work in preparation:

Approximations for the distribution of the longest monotone run, using a scan statistics approach.
Approximations for multidimensional continuous scan statistics of Poisson processes (with C. Preda).



PhD thesis
Approximations for multidimensional discrete scan statistics, Université Lille 1 – Sciences et Technologies, defended in September 2014. Advisor: Prof. Cristian Preda. Referees: Joseph Glaz, Claude Lefèvre. Committee: Stéphane Robin, Azzouz Dermoune, George Haiman, Manuela Sidoroff.


Software
Scan Statistics Simulator: a MATLAB graphical interface for estimating the distribution of the discrete scan statistic in one, two and three dimensions, for several models of the underlying random field. The code will be published on GitHub.


Reviewing and memberships
Reviewer for Methodology and Computing in Applied Probability, Physica A, Statistics & Probability Letters, Romanian Journal of Information Science and Technology and Mathematical Reports.
Member of the Romanian Society of Probability and Statistics and associate member of the Romanian team of The R Project for Statistical Computing.
